brief.head: Power, not bombs
brief.text: Twenty-four coun­tries have nu­clear power and have never built a bomb, Amit Varma said. The two were fused in the 1970s peace and en­vi­ron­men­tal move­ments. {078-C02}

brief.head: Three sources of risk
brief.text: Radioactive ma­te­rial that trav­els thou­sands of kilo­me­tres, run­away chain re­ac­tions and com­plex sys­tems where small human er­rors grow: Ajay Shah’s three sources of nu­clear risk. {078-C03}

brief.head: The sun clocks off
brief.text: Solar is un­beat­able while the sun shines, Ajay Shah said, but it sets just as peo­ple get home[[x3]]. Investors who doubt stor­age can bet on nu­clear. {078-C09}

brief.head: Blame the driver
brief.text: Indian law makes a reactor’s ven­dor li­able for­ever, Ajay Shah said, so no global ven­dor will sell. Like a car, a re­ac­tor should be­come the operator’s re­spon­si­bil­ity after han­dover. {078-C11}

brief.head: Between friends
brief.text: By Ajay Shah’s sums, a 50 MW plant serves about 25,000 house­holds. He rounded a home’s 2,000 watts down to 1,000, be­cause “we don’t want pesky lit­tle de­tails”. {078-J06}

thought.label: Thought for the day
thought.text: You face a prob­lem, that doesn’t mean you stop. It means you try harder.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, on why nuclear safety is a matter of clever engineering

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah make the nuclear case
lead.head: Set the atom free

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 78

play.label: Hear the case in five parts

body: Nuclear power has grown up under a dark cloud, Amit Varma ar­gued, but the facts are com­pletely dif­fer­ent. “Nuclear en­ergy is the safest form of en­ergy known to man,” he said. {078-C01}

Three Mile Island killed no one[[x1]]. At Fukushima, peo­ple died be­cause of the tsunami and a hur­ried evac­u­a­tion, not be­cause of the nu­clear mishap. Chernobyl did kill peo­ple, though the num­bers are dis­puted.
Even on the most neg­a­tive es­ti­mate, Varma said, fewer peo­ple have died in sixty years of nu­clear en­ergy than in a month of ac­ci­dents re­lated to coal.

France, he said, gets 71 per cent of its power from nu­clear en­ergy, has had no safety is­sues and has brought costs down dra­mat­i­cally. Sixty years of nu­clear waste could fit in an un­der­ground bunker the size of a Walmart.

Why, then, has the world held back? Ajay Shah, re­port­ing work done with his co-author Akshay Jaitly, named two rea­sons, fear and cost, and ar­gued that both have largely been solved or are within reach of being solved.
## Counting the dead

On fear, Shah asked for a sense of pro­por­tion. Adding nu­clear power means adding some nu­clear risk to the world and re­mov­ing some coal risk, and coal is the dirt­i­est source of all, on pol­lu­tion, car­bon diox­ide and deaths.

Count ex­cess deaths per megawatt-hour, he said, and nu­clear wins. Spectacular ac­ci­dents, like plane crashes, make head­lines, and that is “mess­ing with our abil­ity to do prob­a­bilis­tic rea­son­ing”. {078-C04}
Safety, Shah ar­gued, is an en­gi­neer­ing prob­lem. The three fa­mous ac­ci­dents all in­volved first-generation de­signs, and many newer re­ac­tors shut them­selves down when some­thing goes wrong.
## A re­ac­tor in a crate
On cost, his an­swer came from the as­sem­bly line. A large plant of 2,000 or 4,000 megawatts takes twenty years to build, and only a hand­ful will ever be made, so it never gets cheaper.
“How do you get the price of a nu­clear re­ac­tor down?” Shah asked. “The an­swer is in­dus­tri­al­i­sa­tion.” {078-C07}
A small mod­u­lar re­ac­tor of 50 or 100 megawatts, about the size of a big truck, could be made by the thou­sand, ar­rive in a crate and be switched on like a factory’s diesel gen­er­a­tor.
Meta and Google, Varma noted, had just placed big or­ders for such re­ac­tors. “We are be­yond the world of the­ory,” he said.
## Freedom to choose
In India, Shah said, ev­ery­thing nu­clear has been treated as the busi­ness of the Department of Atomic Energy, and nuclear’s share of the country’s en­ergy has stayed mi­nus­cule.

He set out five con­di­tions for change: free­dom for pri­vate Indians to im­port plants; free­dom to sell power di­rectly to in­dus­trial and com­mer­cial buy­ers; CISF se­cu­rity on the air­port model; com­pli­ance with the International Atomic Energy Agency’s stan­dards; and a fix to civil nu­clear li­a­bil­ity law. {078-C10}
The hosts, Varma stressed, “have not made an ar­gu­ment for ac­tion. We have made an ar­gu­ment for free­dom.” {078-C12}

Private play­ers should weigh solar, wind, stor­age and nu­clear by their own logic. If the gov­ern­ment truly reg­u­lated for safety, Varma added, it would man­date nu­clear power, and the hosts did not want that ei­ther.

Could India, short of what Shah calls in­vis­i­ble in­fra­struc­ture, man­age any of this, Varma asked. Shah ad­mit­ted the path would be dif­fi­cult. “I have no il­lu­sions that there’s a smooth path to these five things,” he said.

second.label: Fukushima, 2011
second.head: If Japan, why not us?
second.deck: Ajay Shah on the meeting that turned Germany against nuclear power

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Angela Merkel’s Fukushima question

body: After Chernobyl, Ajay Shah said, a lib­eral democ­racy could tell it­self that the dis­as­ter was a Soviet fail­ure, and that a free so­ci­ety would make bet­ter de­ci­sions. Fukushima, in 2011, ended that com­fort.

Angela Merkel, then head of Germany, called a meet­ing after Fukushima around one sen­tence: the Japanese are as good as us; if a nu­clear ac­ci­dent hap­pened there, can it hap­pen here? {#merkel} Merkel, he noted, has a PhD in chem­istry and could rea­son about prob­a­bil­i­ties.

The German logic was sim­ple. Germans saw them­selves as bet­ter en­gi­neers than the Soviets, but not bet­ter than the Japanese. {078-S01} Germany de­cided to shut down all its nu­clear en­ergy, and seen from 2024, Shah said, that was not such a great de­ci­sion.

quote.text: So if an ac­ci­dent could hap­pen in Japan, could it hap­pen in Germany?

third.head: Fear has a body count

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the deaths caused by fear

body: Not using nu­clear en­ergy can cost lives, Amit Varma ar­gued. He re­called Ajay Shah’s point, made be­fore record­ing: after Fukushima, the re­ac­tor was shut down and Japan shifted to coal, and there were deaths be­cause of that. {078-S06}
“So ac­tu­ally it wasn’t the nu­clear en­ergy per se or that ac­ci­dent that caused deaths,” Varma said. “It was then stop­ping to use it, get­ting car­ried away that caused fur­ther deaths.”

He added a fact he half-remembered. After 9/11, when se­cu­rity mea­sures went up and peo­ple were scared, they drove more and flew less, and mor­tal­ity went up, be­cause more peo­ple die in car ac­ci­dents than in plane crashes, by an order of mag­ni­tude.
Shah had made a re­lated point ear­lier: plane crashes make head­lines, but fly­ing from Bombay to Delhi is far safer[[x2]] than driv­ing. {078-C04}

box.title: The paper behind the episode
box.text: Everything Ajay Shah re­ported, he said, was joint work with his co-author Akshay Jaitly. Their ar­ti­cle on it came out, Amit Varma noted, in prac­ti­cally the same week that Meta and Google placed big or­ders for small mod­u­lar re­ac­tors. {078-J14}

sections.label: The history
sections.head: Endless energy, endless delays
sections.caption: why nuclear power stumbled
body: In 1945, Ajay Shah said, the mood was a bound­less op­ti­mism that hu­man­ity had fig­ured out the whole thing and there would be end­less free en­ergy[[x5]]. In prac­tice, nu­clear en­ergy has been a dis­ap­point­ment world­wide.

It proved ex­tremely cap­i­tal in­ten­sive, partly be­cause the equip­ment is ex­pen­sive and partly be­cause of de­lays in con­struc­tion. A mod­ern large plant of two or four thou­sand megawatts takes twenty years to build. {#twentyyears} Add up the eco­nom­ics, Shah said, and it looks ter­ri­ble.
## Blame the sys­tem

Then came the fear. When Chernobyl hap­pened, many peo­ple ex­plained it away as the mon­u­men­tal stu­pid­ity and sys­temic fail­ure[[x4]] of the Soviet Union, where peo­ple afraid of being sent to Siberia kept mak­ing wrong de­ci­sions. “Authoritarian sys­tems make peo­ple stupid and they make mis­takes,” as Shah put it. {078-C06}

He pointed to HBO’s *Chernobyl* as a text­book ac­count of how a big op­pres­sive state fails, with noth­ing to do with nu­clear power. The Soviets, he added, never re­ally fig­ured out air­craft car­ri­ers or sub­marines ei­ther.
The hope that a lib­eral democ­racy would do bet­ter lasted until Fukushima in 2011, which shook even Angela Merkel’s Germany into shut­ting down all its nu­clear en­ergy.

~ This, for Shah, is the cri­sis of nu­clear en­ergy: a bound­less source of power that fails hard dol­lars-and-cents cal­cu­la­tions, with the loom­ing prob­lem of safety on top. The hosts argue that both prob­lems are largely solved or within reach.

quote.text: We are not bet­ter en­gi­neers than the Japanese. We are bet­ter en­gi­neers than the Soviets.

sections.label: Safety
sections.head: The real killer is coal
sections.caption: the safety of nuclear reactors
body: Ajay Shah went back to first prin­ci­ples. Three things, he said, came to­gether in the fa­mous dis­as­ters. Radioactive ma­te­rial is a dif­fer­ent game: a gas re­lease trav­els thou­sands of kilo­me­tres, comes down as ra­dioac­tive rain and trig­gers birth de­fects.

A run­away chain re­ac­tion can melt hun­dreds of me­tres into the ground and con­tam­i­nate ground­wa­ter. And a re­ac­tor is a com­plex sys­tem, where a human error can mag­nify into some­thing much big­ger. {078-C03}
Even so, count sixty years of ex­cess deaths and the num­bers are mod­est. “The killer is coal[[x6]],” Shah said, “and you haven’t even started count­ing cli­mate change yet.”
## Unsafe at any speed

Nor are these prob­lems fixed for ever. In 1965, Shah re­called, Ralph Nader’s *Unsafe at Any Speed* doc­u­mented the dan­gers of American cars, and rev­o­lu­tion­ary gains in car safety fol­lowed. {078-J13}

Many im­proved re­ac­tor de­signs sim­ply shut them­selves down in a safety in­ci­dent, as forces like grav­ity pull the fis­sile ma­te­rial apart. There can be no run­away chain re­ac­tion. {078-C05}
~ The proof, Shah said, is al­ready at sea: the re­ac­tors on the air­craft car­ri­ers and sub­marines of ad­vanced economies have run for decades with­out a safety in­ci­dent.

quote.text: This is the heart of the idea that it’s about clever en­gi­neer­ing.

sections.label: Small reactors
sections.head: Reactors off the assembly line
sections.caption: small modular reactors
body: To show how nu­clear power can get cheap, Ajay Shah went back to the Second World War, when as­sem­bly-line ships beat the U-boats and mass-produced Sherman tanks over­whelmed the Tiger. Scale and learn­ing, he ar­gued, beat crafts­man­ship[[x8]].

A 4,000 megawatt re­ac­tor will only ever be made in a hand­ful, he said, so it can­not be in­dus­tri­alised. At 50 or 100 megawatts[[x7]] you can think of mak­ing a thou­sand, or ten thou­sand, with every com­po­nent mass-produced. {078-C07}

Such a re­ac­tor, about 30 per cent big­ger than the big­gest truck, would come in a crate. Place it on site, throw a switch, and it runs like the diesel gen sets so many Indian fac­to­ries al­ready have.
## The solar prece­dent

Solar, Shah said, has had one of the great­est cost col­lapses in world his­tory, be­cause its man­u­fac­tur­ing has just two sim­ple steps. The first, polysil­i­con, is a scale busi­ness: “There are only ten fac­to­ries in the world who do this at scale.” {#tenfactories}
~ Amit Varma spot­ted an irony. “This is an ar­ti­sanal show. We are both ar­ti­sans,” he said, and here was Shah telling ev­ery­one not to do im­por­tant things the ar­ti­sanal way. {078-J05}

quote.text: And if there is to be any fu­ture in nu­clear, it will come be­cause of man­u­fac­tur­ing that will crash prices of SMRs.

sections.label: The Indian story
sections.head: Power plants are a business
sections.caption: nuclear power as a business
body: Just as in space re­search, Ajay Shah said, India as­sumed that nu­clear work could only be done by the gov­ern­ment. That was de­bat­able even in 1945 or 1955. Today it is very wrong.

He wants weapons and en­ergy de­cou­pled. Steel for guns and ar­tillery shells is a de­fence busi­ness, where strate­gic au­ton­omy mat­ters. In en­ergy, India is a nor­mal part of glob­al­i­sa­tion: Bharat Heavy Electricals makes gen­er­a­tion equip­ment, but im­ported equip­ment com­petes with it.

Nuclear power should work the same way. L&T could ask whether to make small re­ac­tors for the world mar­ket; Tata Power or Reliance Energy could buy a nu­clear gen­er­at­ing sta­tion; Hindalco could buy a French re­ac­tor for cap­tive power. “It is con­gen­i­tally not pos­si­ble for the Indian State to do any­thing ef­fi­ciently,” Shah said. {078-C08}
## A share that never grew

The gov­ern­ment ap­proach, he said, has not worked: nuclear’s share of Indian en­ergy con­sump­tion is mi­nus­cule and has not grown. He made the same case against hand­ing dig­i­tal pub­lic goods to a pub­lic sec­tor com­pany.
~ Amit Varma rec­om­mended Jahnavi Phalkey’s *Atomic State*, on the early pi­o­neers of nu­clear sci­ence in India, and his con­ver­sa­tion with her, *Jahnavi and the Cyclotron*. {078-R05}

quote.text: Building nu­clear re­ac­tors is a busi­ness. It’s a nor­mal pri­vate busi­ness with some in­ter­play with the gov­ern­ment

sections.label: Five conditions
sections.head: Five knots to untie
sections.caption: five conditions for nuclear freedom
body: Ajay Shah listed five prob­lems the Indian state must work on. The first: pri­vate Indians must be free to de­cide to im­port a nu­clear plant. {078-C10}
A 50 megawatt plant, he said, costs about two to three hun­dred mil­lion dol­lars, or Rs 1,500 to 2,500 crore, within the means of India’s top hun­dred com­pa­nies.

Second, own­ers must be free to sell power di­rectly to in­dus­trial and com­mer­cial buy­ers, keep­ing out the dis­tri­bu­tion com­pa­nies, which think nu­clear too ex­pen­sive. Offshore wind de­vel­op­ers al­ready have that free­dom.

Third, se­cu­rity on the air­port model. Private air­lines fly in and out of pri­vate air­ports, while the gov­ern­ment runs avi­a­tion se­cu­rity. At nu­clear plants, the CISF would guard the ura­nium and the waste under clear pro­to­cols, at the operator’s cost. {#cisf}
## Who an­swers for ac­ci­dents
Fourth, India must sign up to and com­ply with the International Atomic Energy Agency’s stan­dards, or the world will not sell it fuel and re­ac­tors.

Fifth, li­a­bil­ity. After you buy a car, the brakes are your re­spon­si­bil­ity. Under the in­ter­na­tional doc­trine, vic­tims sue only the op­er­a­tor, who alone may sue the ven­dor over a de­sign de­fect. {078-C11}
~ Indian law in­stead makes the ven­dor li­able for­ever, and so, Shah said, no global firm will sell a re­ac­tor to an Indian buyer.

quote.text: There’s a han­dover date, and then re­spon­si­bil­ity shifts to the op­er­a­tor.

sections.label: The argument
sections.head: Permission, not a push
sections.caption: freedom, not action
body: Amit Varma drew the threads to­gether. The hosts were not telling pri­vate com­pa­nies to go and in­vest in nu­clear, nor the Indian state to solve the power prob­lem. They asked only that the state stop shut­ting it out. {078-C12}
It is not the job of thinkers or pol­i­cy­mak­ers, Ajay Shah had said, to plan cen­trally that there will be 5,000 megawatts of nu­clear. {#central}

Varma had added a twist ear­lier. If the gov­ern­ment re­ally reg­u­lated on safety grounds, it would man­date nu­clear power, since it is far safer than any other kind in use. The hosts did not want that ei­ther. {078-J09}
## Invisible in­fra­struc­ture

Then Varma pressed Shah. India, he wor­ried, lacks the in­vis­i­ble in­fra­struc­ture[[x9]], the bet­ter rule of law and pro­cesses honed over decades, that lets such mod­els work in the West. The state might hand the sec­tor to a crony, botch the se­cu­rity, or turn any small role into rent-seeking.

Shah called these fair con­cerns and ad­mit­ted the path would be dif­fi­cult. His an­swer, from their episode *The Long Road to Change*, is a vi­brant in­tel­lec­tual land­scape of thinkers, re­searchers and crit­ics that pulls a fum­bling state back when­ever it goes too far ei­ther way. {078-C13}
~ “Out of that,” he said, “we be­come a bet­ter coun­try.”

quote.text: The an­swer lies in knowl­edge and com­mu­nity that we need enough peo­ple in India who think, who write, who de­bate, who crit­i­cise.
We are not ar­gu­ing for ac­tion. We are ar­gu­ing for free­dom, that this is in­cred­i­ble. Let’s not shut it out with state ac­tion that gets in the way.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: U-boats, Tiger tanks, a bomb built from scratch and a ministry’s early calculations

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the Battle of the Atlantic, and what it teaches
stories.head: You sink them, we’ll build more
body: “All the great sto­ries of the world begin at the Second World War,” Ajay Shah an­nounced, and flew back to 1941. {078-J02}

The Battle of the Atlantic was under way. German sub­marines, the so-called U-boats, were sink­ing the ships that car­ried food, weapons and mil­i­tary sup­plies from America to Britain. Britain was an is­land: cut its link to America, and you stran­gled its abil­ity to re­sist.
Hundreds of ships were lost. The hosts reached for a Bob Dylan song and asked how many ships the U-boats must shoot down be­fore the British have no food. {078-J03}

The an­swer began with a medi­ocre British de­sign of about ten thou­sand tons, af­fec­tion­ately called the ugly duck­ling. Ships had al­ways been ar­ti­sanal: peo­ple put the pieces to­gether bit by bit, and each one came out dif­fer­ent. The Americans de­cided to mass-produce this one, Henry Ford style, on as­sem­bly lines at 18 ship­yards. {#shipyards}
Then came the gains from learn­ing. At the be­gin­ning it took 270 days to com­mis­sion a ship; by the end, it took 35. {#shipdays} In all, 2,700 ships were built, and the price crashed.

The mes­sage to the Germans, as Shah put it: “You keep shoot­ing down our ships, we’ll make even more of the ships.” {078-S02} Mighty American man­u­fac­tur­ing was big­ger than any sub­marines Germany could put into the sea.

~ Shah thinks the bat­tle is un­der­rated: one of the most in­ter­est­ing sto­ries of the war, about how in­ge­nu­ity, ef­fort, imag­i­na­tion and cre­ativ­ity came to­gether. Perhaps, he said, it de­serves an episode of its own.
stories.why: Scale and the learn­ing curve beat crafts­man­ship. Shah’s point is that nu­clear power can get cheap the same way: build small re­ac­tors by the thou­sand on as­sem­bly lines, in­stead of one-off giant plants. {078-C07}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the ugly duckling ships

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on craftsmen, assembly lines and the Tiger
stories.head: A tank too finely made
body: The German Tiger tank was a great tank, Ajay Shah said. Its trou­ble, he said, was that it was an ar­ti­sanal prod­uct[[x10]].

“Every eleven Tiger tanks that were pro­duced, there would be a change in the de­sign,” he said. “Because the peo­ple mak­ing those tanks were mas­ter crafts­men. And that’s dumb. It drives up the cost.” {078-S03}
What you want, Shah said, is a fac­tory that just mass-produces the de­sign. The Americans did that with the Sherman tank[[x11]], and then taught the Soviets how to do it with the T-34.
~ Together, he said, they blew away German man­u­fac­tur­ing by a fac­tor of ten. It was the same les­son as the ships, and the one Shah would apply to nu­clear re­ac­tors.
stories.why: Constant tin­ker­ing by ex­perts is the enemy of cost re­duc­tion. A stan­dard­ised, good-enough de­sign, pro­duced at vol­ume, wins wars, and Shah ar­gues it can win mar­kets for nu­clear re­ac­tors too.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the Tiger and the Sherman

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on India’s 1974 test, and why power is different
stories.head: The bomb India built alone
body: Most nu­clear pow­ers got there through leaks, Ajay Shah said. The Soviets stole se­crets from the Manhattan Project; the Soviets passed them to the Chinese, and the Chinese to the North Koreans and the Pakistanis.

India was dif­fer­ent. It went from scratch to a nu­clear test in 1974, with­out any pro­lif­er­a­tion. Shah cred­ited the glory days of Homi Bhabha, Raja Ramanna, Sethna and their col­leagues. “More power to them,” he said. {078-S04}

But build­ing ef­fi­cient, cheap nu­clear en­ergy, he said, is a dif­fer­ent prob­lem, closer to the work of Bharat Heavy Electricals: an or­di­nary in­dus­trial prob­lem of scale and unit eco­nom­ics.

~ “This is not some­thing that fits well in the Indian state,” Shah said. India as­sumed ev­ery­thing nu­clear be­longed to the Department of Atomic Energy, he ar­gued, and nuclear’s share has stayed mi­nus­cule.

quote.text: India is one of the few coun­tries which fig­ured this out en­tirely alone.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on India’s 1974 nuclear test

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s early sums at the Ministry of Finance
stories.head: A reactor that failed the sums
body: When Ajay Shah was at the Ministry of Finance, he started on some early cal­cu­la­tions about India’s gov­ern­ment-run nu­clear power plants. They told him, he said, “that this isn’t going any­where”. {078-S05}
Measure the cost cor­rectly, he found, and there was just no way those plants could play a mean­ing­ful role in the Indian en­ergy mix. The ef­fi­ciency was not there.
Even then it was clear, Shah said, that the top-of-the-line French and American re­ac­tors were very, very cost ef­fi­cient com­pared with what hap­pened here.

~ The share of nu­clear en­ergy in Indian en­ergy con­sump­tion, he said, re­mains mi­nus­cule and has not grown over the years. In his dream, for­eign firms would sell re­ac­tors to pri­vate Indian buy­ers, with Indian en­gi­neer­ing firms join­ing them after five, ten or twenty years. {#dream}
stories.why: The trou­ble with Indian nu­clear power was never only the fear of ac­ci­dents. A state mo­nop­oly, Shah ar­gued, sim­ply could not de­liver com­pet­i­tive eco­nom­ics, which is why he wants the de­ci­sions left to pri­vate firms. {078-C08}

quiz.q: In what year did India conduct its nuclear test, and how unusually?
quiz.a: 1974, and it fig­ured it out en­tirely alone, with no leaked se­crets.

quiz.q: Why does the sun pose a problem for a solar power system, in Shah’s telling?
quiz.a: It sets every evening, just as peo­ple get home and switch things on.

quiz.q: Under the international doctrine, whom do victims of a nuclear accident sue?
quiz.a: Only the op­er­a­tor, who alone may then sue the ven­dor over de­sign de­fects.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 78. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Angela Merkel (Armin Linnartz, CC BY-SA 3.0 de); Ralph Nader (https://www.flickr.com/photos/wickenden/ Don LaVange, CC BY-SA 2.0); Steven Pinker (Christopher Michel, CC BY-SA 4.0); Marvin Gaye (Wikimedia Commons, public domain). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon and Wikipedia.

shelf.title: Nuclear Power Can Save the World
shelf.creator: Joshua S Goldstein, Staffan A Qvist & Steven Pinker
shelf.why: The data be­hind the hosts’ case for nu­clear power: sixty years of nu­clear deaths, Chernobyl in­cluded, roughly equal one month of coal-related deaths, and 60 years of American nu­clear waste could fit in a sin­gle Walmart.

shelf.title: Chernobyl
shelf.creator: HBO
shelf.why: It is a text­book ac­count of how a big op­pres­sive state fails, which shows the dis­as­ter was about the po­lit­i­cal sys­tem rather than nu­clear physics.

shelf.title: Midnight in Chernobyl
shelf.creator: Adam Higginbotham
shelf.why: Gripping re­portage on what hap­pened be­hind the scenes at Chernobyl, show­ing the dis­as­ter as a fail­ure of the Soviet state, rooted in its struc­ture and in­cen­tives so that it seems bound to hap­pen.

shelf.title: Atomic State: Big Science In Twentieth-century India
shelf.creator: Jahnavi Phalkey
shelf.why: Jahnavi Phalkey’s his­tory of the early pi­o­neers of nu­clear sci­ence in India, in­clud­ing the 1940s strug­gle among three sci­en­tists in which one won out and the other two didn’t.

shelf.title: Jahnavi and the Cyclotron (Episode 319, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Jahnavi Phalkey
shelf.why: Jahnavi Phalkey on a 1940s tus­sle among three sci­en­tists over build­ing India’s physics in­sti­tu­tions, which shows nor­mal pol­i­tics re­turn­ing once ex­tra­or­di­nary times end.

shelf.title: The Brave New Future of Electricity (Episode 40, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on the power sec­tor: solar, wind, stor­age and time-of-day pric­ing, why elec­tric­ity prices must be al­lowed to move, and why fix­ing Indian power is a 25-year jour­ney that Indian man­u­fac­tur­ing de­pends on.

shelf.title: Climate Change and Our Power Sector (Episode 278, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Akshay Jaitly and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Akshay Jaitly and Ajay on cli­mate change and India’s power sec­tor, cen­tred on the elec­tric­ity grid: the con­ver­sa­tional ver­sion of their case for re­form­ing elec­tric­ity.

shelf.title: Making the way for nuclear energy in India
shelf.creator: Akshay Jaitly and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit calls it fan­tas­tic and ‘most ex­cel­lent reading’.

shelf.title: A new dawn for nuclear energy?
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s writ­ing on nu­clear en­ergy, be­hind his op­ti­mism and his ar­gu­ment for sep­a­rat­ing nu­clear weapons from nu­clear power and treat­ing re­ac­tors as a busi­ness.

shelf.title: The Long Road to Change (Episode 36, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ the­ory of change: pol­icy im­proves through a decades-long pipe­line of data, re­search, rival pro­pos­als, pub­lic de­bate, com­mit­tee re­ports and draft laws, not by whis­per­ing in a joint secretary’s ear.

shelf.title: The Problem With Digital Public Goods (Episode 56, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A cri­tique of ‘dig­i­tal pub­lic infrastructure’ such as Aadhaar and UPI: state-backed mo­nop­o­lies cre­ated by co­er­cive power, with­out checks and bal­ances, that crowd out com­pet­ing pri­vate sys­tems.

shelf.title: The Battle of the Atlantic
shelf.why: He thinks it is un­der­rated and one of the most in­ter­est­ing sto­ries of the Second World War, about how in­ge­nu­ity, ef­fort, imag­i­na­tion and cre­ativ­ity to­gether won the bat­tle for the Allies.

shelf.title: Paul
shelf.creator: Big Thief
shelf.why: A self-described old fogey whose music is ‘all ancient’, he is amazed to have found a song from as re­cently as 2016 that he ab­so­lutely loves.

shelf.title: Wherever I Lay My Hat (That’s My Home)
shelf.creator: Marvin Gaye (original); Paul Young (cover)
shelf.why: A song Amit calls a mas­ter­piece, es­pe­cially in Paul Young’s cover, which cap­tures his idea of a por­ta­ble home you carry with you (though he has lost every hat he’s owned).

laughs.text: The open­ing: at a re­cent con­fer­ence three dif­fer­ent peo­ple walked up to Ajay and called him Amit. A rat­tled Ajay mes­saged Amit ask­ing ‘Do peo­ple call you Ajay?’ Amit’s reply: ‘No, bro, never hap­pened to me, must be some­thing with you.’

Amit, after Ajay’s case against ar­ti­sanal pro­duc­tion: ‘this is an ar­ti­sanal show. We are both ar­ti­sans. If not artists, we can have delu­sions about that.’ So it’s ironic, he says, to hear Ajay say don’t do im­por­tant things the ar­ti­sanal way.

Ajay’s house­hold power maths: a home draws about two thou­sand watts, but ‘be­tween friends, I’m gonna call it a thousand’, be­cause ‘to do good oral cal­cu­la­tions, we don’t want pesky lit­tle de­tails.’
Amit siz­ing a 50 MW re­ac­tor in Mumbai terms: ‘not Andheri size, maybe Versova size, def­i­nitely Yari Road size.’

Ajay says the sun has ‘an un­pleas­ant habit of set­ting every evening.’ Amit later cor­rects him in Hindi: ‘Ki sir, sun­set nahi ho raha, hum ghoom rahe’ (‘Sir, the sun isn’t set­ting, we’re the ones turning’).
The sign-off: ‘Where is your home, Ajay Shah? Your spir­i­tual home, your in­tel­lec­tual home.’ The an­swer: ‘Bandra East.’
During the Battle of the Atlantic story the hosts reach for ‘a Bob Dylan song’ and sing their own ver­sion about how many ships the U-boats must shoot down ‘be­fore the British have no food.’

Ralph Nader’s ‘Unsafe at Any Speed’ (1965), which doc­u­mented the dan­gers of American cars. Ajay uses it to argue that ex­pos­ing a technology’s flaws leads to en­gi­neer­ing fixes, not to aban­don­ing the tech­nol­ogy.

Meta (aka Facebook) and Google plac­ing big or­ders for small mod­u­lar re­ac­tors in prac­ti­cally the same week Ajay and Akshay Jaitly’s ar­ti­cle came out. Amit: ‘We are be­yond the world of the­ory.’
